description: We are a team of prospective graduates from Singapore who are keen to utilize NASA NISAR capabilities to enhance the quality of life of our fellow ASEAN peers. We love eating rice and we love data analytics. Check out NISAR Rice Globe at https://jshchong.github.io/NISAR-FINAL/ now!
summary:
Problem:
In Southeast Asia, rice planting relies on monsoon. When rains arrive late, farmers plant late, threatening harvests and food supply. Ground surveys are slow and monsoon clouds blind optical satellites.

Solution: 
Our interactive 3D NISAR Rice Globe uses NISAR L-band radar to map rice growth stage and planting timing across regions. Radar works through monsoon, day or night, whereas optical satellites don't.

How it works: 
NISAR L2 GCOV data (HH and HV) comes from ASF DAAC. HV backscatter rises as the canopy grows, then levels off near maturity and drops at harvest. A Python pipeline detects rice from this signature, filters false positives like fish ponds, and estimates crop age and stage. Each field’s planting date is compared with its region’s recommended window. 

Who it’s for:
When the globe shows a region still unplanted as its planting window closes, the government can help by sending seeds and fertiliser support, promote other varieties, and deploy extension officers, agronomists and irrigation technicians.  

Limitations:
No field validation yet, with stage and timing good to about ±2–3 weeks. 
The time series is short (9–11 images) with a Jul–Aug gap.
Crop types may be distinguished inaccurately.

Future applications: 
The method could extend to other crops such as sugarcane using specific backscatter thresholds. Flooding and soil moisture datasets could support water management by showing irrigation demand to save water and support flood monitoring.
details:
1. Problem and aim

Monsoon cloud hides Southeast Asian paddies from optical satellites for months, which is exactly when rice is planted. NISAR's radar sees through cloud, day and night.

The project turns NISAR observations into three things farmers, agencies and insurers can act on:

  1. Growth stage of every field: flooded or freshly planted, growing, or ready for harvest.
  2. Estimated planting date of every field.
  3. Planting timing against the region's recommended window: early, on time or late.

2. How L-band radar sees rice

NISAR's L-band wavelength (~24 cm) passes through the canopy. Two polarisations carry the signal:

  • HV measures leafy volume, so it rises as the crop grows.
  • HH is strongest when water and upright stems bounce the pulse back (double bounce).

Following both over time reveals the crop cycle.

Figure 1. HV through one rice crop.

  • A (schematic): anchored to measured values.
  • B (measured): NISAR medians across four regions.
  • The pattern: flooded paddies sit near −22 dB, then HV climbs about 6 dB to a plateau near −16 dB and falls at harvest.

3. Method

Each 30 m pixel is classified from its time series, not from one image

Figure 2. Processing pipeline. Everything is pre-computed in Python, so the website only loads finished image frames and a JSON index.

Classification rules

  • Rice test: the field's seasonal HV low point is ≤ −18 dB, then HV rises ≥ 3 dB (the "green-up").
    • Flooded / freshly planted: HV at its low point with HH ≤ −15 dB after an earlier crop, or a crop only just visible.
    • Growing: crop age below the region's maturity threshold, or HV still rising ≥ 2 dB.
    • Ready: crop age above the threshold and HV within 3 dB of its peak.

Planting date and timing

Estimated planting date = first green-up date − regional radar delay

Each field's estimate is compared with its region's recommended window, with a ±12-day tolerance (one NISAR cycle). It is then classed as early, on time or late, or as not yet planted (window open) or no planting detected (window closed).

4. NASA data

  • Product: NISAR Level-2 GCOV (Geocoded Polarimetric Covariance), layers HHHH and HVHV (radiometrically terrain-corrected backscatter, 10–20 m), from NASA Earthdata / ASF DAAC.
  • Collections: PROVISIONAL (from 17 Jun 2026) and VALIDATED (from 21 Oct 2026).
  • Processing: only each region's 27 km box was streamed, then averaged to 30 m. The 30 m map resolution is ours; it is not the native product resolution.
  • Data gap: NISAR collected no data at all from 27 Jul to 10 Aug 2026.

Figure 3. NISAR passes used per region. Blue dots are PROVISIONAL products and green dots are VALIDATED. The shaded band is NISAR's permanent data gap.

5. Regions and planting calendars

Windows come from official 2026 schedules where published and from typical crop calendars elsewhere (mostly FAO GIEWS). Thai Binh uses neighbouring Hai Phong's 2026 plan as a proxy.

Figure 4. The 14 regions. Stars mark regions with an official 2026 planting schedule.

Figure 5. Where the windows come from, and the calendar check (whether each region's stage mix fits its crop calendar). The calendar check is a plausibility test, not an accuracy measure.

6. Results

Each region is shown as of its latest NISAR pass (22 Oct – 6 Nov 2026).

Figure 6. One season in Nueva Ecija, read from four NISAR passes.

  • 22 Aug: 97% flooded.
  • 15 Sep: 79% growing.
  • 9 Oct: 31% ready.
  • 2 Nov: 57% ready, with gaps where fields are already harvested.

Figure 7. Growth stage by region.

  • Mostly ready or harvested: Central Luzon.
  • Growing toward harvest: Isan and Battambang.
  • Re-flooding for the next crop (blue): Karawang and MADA.

Figure 8. Planting timing against each region's window.

  • Late: about a third of An Giang planted late, and Nueva Ecija's late fields cluster in the north-west.
  • Still open: Java's and MADA's windows run to November–December, so many fields are still "not yet planted".
  • Use caution: Thai Binh's high "late" share is flagged as unreliable.

7. The application

A static website on GitHub Pages: CesiumJS 1.120.0 renders the globe over Esri World Imagery and place labels. A timeline steps through NISAR's 12-day cycles. If a region has no pass in the selected cycle, its previous image is shown at reduced opacity.

8. Limitations and next steps

  • Rice vs other crops:
    • The rice test does not yet require a flood signature, so short-cycle crops such as cassava or maize may be included, mainly in Isan and Ngawi.
    • Next: add a flood requirement and cross-check against Southeast Asian rice maps (NESEA-Rice10, the Philippines' PRiSM) and national planted-area statistics.
    • 9–11 passes per region, plus the July–August data gap.
    • The newest stage often rests on one image, and carried-forward frames can be up to 24 days old.

The NISAR Rice Globe is an experimental monitoring platform, not a validated rice census.

9. Conclusion

Tracking how NISAR's HH and HV signals change every 12 days lets the globe show what stage each field is in, when it was planted, and whether that was on time, across 14 Southeast Asian rice regions in cloudy monsoon conditions.

With flood-signature filtering and ground validation, the same pipeline could scale to whole provinces and update automatically with every NISAR pass.
